title: Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of reinforcement learning from a computer science perspective. It introduces the central problem of an agent learning through trial-and-error interaction with a dynamic environment, and it distinguishes reinforcement learning from supervised learning and related areas such as search, planning, and adaptive control. The paper is not an empirical study; instead, it organizes the field and reviews major concepts, algorithms, and theoretical results.

A major focus is the problem of choosing actions under uncertainty when rewards may be immediate or delayed. The paper explains the standard reinforcement-learning model, models of optimal behavior (finite-horizon, discounted infinite-horizon, and average-reward), and criteria for evaluating learning algorithms such as convergence speed and regret. It then reviews classical techniques for exploration in the simple bandit setting, including dynamic-programming-based methods, Gittins indices, learning automata, greedy and randomized heuristics, and interval-based methods.

The paper further surveys delayed-reward methods for Markov decision processes, including value iteration, policy iteration, modified policy iteration, temporal-difference learning, TD(bb), Q-learning, and average-reward extensions. It also discusses model-based approaches such as certainty equivalence and Dyna. Its main conclusion is that reinforcement learning had strong theoretical foundations but remained challenged by exploration, delayed credit assignment, and scalability to large state spaces.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a 1996 survey/theoretical review of reinforcement learning, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It contains no K-12 learner sample, no experimental design, and no measured educational outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate educational impact, only summarizes RL methods and theory. There are no reported effects on student achievement, retention, engagement, or institutional outcomes.
